Subject: Sizing options for regulated inference (private vs dedicated)

Hi Emma,

Thanks again for the call this morning — really appreciate the walkthrough of Catalyst Health's telemetry and the compliance constraints for patient data residency. Per our conversation, teams at organizations like yours typically choose between two inference deployment modes: Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) and Redwood Private (VPC / customer-managed control plane).

I attached a short checklist matrix that highlights the practical differences, but high level:
- Dedicated: predictable throughput, simpler onboarding, shared control plane; easier for burst capacity but requires strong network controls if data residency is required.
- Private: full control of network and key management, better for strict audit/regulatory workflows, slightly longer setup and higher fixed cost.

To produce an apples-to-apples capacity estimate we need a couple of workload signals from your side: average concurrent requests at peak, average request token length, expected 95th percentile latency target, and whether real-time inference or batched async jobs are primary. You mentioned a mix of low-latency chat for clinicians and large-batch codex-style summarization. If you can send the Q2 workload export (CSV) and your procurement contact, I’ll loop in SRE and pricing.

Next steps I propose:
1) Send over the workload CSV and named procurement contact (if not already on this thread).
2) We’ll run quick capacity simulations for both Dedicated and Private and return a side-by-side with estimated GPU counts, expected token-per-second throughput, and cost bands.
3) If Private is the preferred route, we’ll include a checklist for KMS/HSM, VPC peering, and SOC2 artifacts.

If it helps, I can also schedule a 30-minute session with Marcus (runtime) and Monica (security) to walk through technical tradeoffs.

Thanks,

Lauren / team,

I ran a quick capacity simulation and sketched out a recommendation (see capacity-recommendation-CH-v1.xlsx attached). High level conclusions:

Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) — conservative config for 250ms p95 chat:
- Model assumption: 13B open checkpoint with q4_0 quant (validated quality/latency tradeoff)
- Per-GPU steady throughput: ~28 concurrent chat streams at 250ms p95 (A100-80GB equivalent with our runtime optimizations and KV cache).
- Required fleet: 8 GPUs for steady-state (220 / 28 = 7.86) + 2 spare for rolling updates => target 10 GPUs.
- Burst profile: autoscale policy (burst capacity) to +40% (up to 14 GPUs) for short windows.
- Cost posture: predictable monthly reserved cost; lower operational complexity.

Private (VPC/customer-managed control plane) — additional considerations:
- Same baseline GPU sizing for inference, but add 15–25% headroom for stricter isolation (network overhead, lack of shared hot cache) => recommend 12–13 GPUs baseline + 2 spare => 14–15 GPUs recommended.
- Batch summarization: schedule to run on off-peak capacity using preemptible spot pools inside the customer's VPC where permitted (saves ~30% cost).
- Network & KMS: for EU residency we assume VPC peering and customer-managed KMS; egress latencies increase 10–30ms depending on regional topology — add to latency budget.
- Operational notes: Private onboarding adds ~4–6 weeks (VPC setup, cert exchanges, SOC2 evidence review) vs Dedicated which is ~1–2 weeks.

Other recommendations:
- Model variants: propose offering two model flavors behind a Smart Routing policy: low-latency q4_0 13B for clinician chat, and higher-quality 13B/70B for large-batch jobs. Fallback to a smaller 7B variant if capacity constrained.
- Caching: enable prefix/KV caching for clinical templates — can reduce token compute by ~18% on average.
- Mx SLOs: monitor p95 token latencies and maintain per-route dashboards.

I attached the spreadsheet with per-GPU throughput assumptions, cost delta estimates, and a 12-month TCO comparison between Dedicated and Private with expected monthly runs. Happy to walk through details on Monday.

—Marcus

Hi Emma / Procurement team,

Thanks for the workload file and for looping procurement. Based on our analysis (summary attached: Private_vs_Dedicated_Comparison_CH.pdf) here are the recommended options tailored to Catalyst's constraints:

Option A — Redwood Dedicated (recommended if time-to-live and lower onboarding effort is primary):
- Fleet: 10 GPUs reserved (A100-80GB equiv), autoscale to 14 GPUs during bursts
- Latency: meets 250ms p95 for clinician chat using q4_0 13B variant + KV cache
- Time to onboard: ~1–2 weeks
- Cost: lower short-term setup cost; monthly reserved pricing shown in attached TCO sheet

Option B — Redwood Private (recommended if strict EU residency and customer-managed KMS are non-negotiable):
- Fleet: 14 GPUs recommended baseline (includes 15% isolation headroom)
- Latency: p95 target achievable but allow 10–30ms extra for VPC peering; recommend additional headroom if network hops exceed 2
- Time to onboard: ~4–6 weeks (VPC peering, KMS/HSM integration, SOC2 evidence handoff)
- Cost: higher fixed baseline; potential savings by routing batch work to preemptible pools inside customer VPC

Requested next steps:
1) Procurement: please review the attached PO-template and confirm billing entity and PO timelines.
2) SRE/Security: John (cc'd earlier) — can you confirm whether Catalyst requires HSM-backed keys or if KMS with customer key rotation is acceptable?
3) Technical run-through: if helpful we can schedule a 30–45 minute session with Marcus & Monica this week to go through the TCO spreadsheet and network checklist.
